### Exact implementation plan

1. Before the existing current=_now(now), initialize only a local reject flag. In a try/except Exception, open a fresh self._relay_session_factory context and perform one indexed SELECT of delivery state and claim_token, joined to RelayMessageRecord, filtered on the exact delivery_id. Select scalar columns, no payload or ORM entity that could leak into the writer identity map.
2. Only state==delivered may set the flag: use the existing _delivery_receipt helper; a null expected digest or a definite false hmac.compare_digest is the existing terminal conflict. Read/digest/comparison Exception means no proof and may fall through only after normal cleanup succeeds. Retain the read Session and its normal SQLAlchemy Connection, without adding a raw/new connection. In finally, close the read Session. If normal close raises Exception, independently attempt captured Connection.invalidate, Connection.close and Session.invalidate as best-effort cleanup, then re-raise the original close failure even if salvage returns normally. Never infer physical release from invalidation success or enter the writer after close failure. Never catch BaseException/cancellation, normalize receipt grammar or log/return tokens/digests. Raise RelayConflictError with the exact existing delivered-mismatch text only after normal read cleanup succeeds.
3. Leave the original current capture and complete writer code unchanged. Matching delivered receipts, claimed/pending/expired/suppressed rows, missing delivery or joined parent, corrupt values, non-ASCII comparison errors and any uncertain preflight use a fresh original writer session and all existing lease/expiry/receipt/state checks. No read-side200 or404, write retry, cache or new scope filter. Correct receipts remain valid across containers as before. No clock replacement or changes to the real-clock redelivery journey/protected assertions.

### Hot-path and resource decision

Every ACK now pays one indexed joined read, with two scalar columns and no payload, before a sequential fresh writer when needed. Normal read cleanup must succeed before writer acquisition; after cleanup failure the request propagates failure and cannot proceed to writer or409, with independent best-effort salvage attempted. SQLAlchemy invalidation can suppress DBAPI close failures, so salvage success is not physical-release proof. There is no new thread, retained cursor, second simultaneous connection, reader-to-writer upgrade or cached decision. Existing factory connections retain their15000ms busy timeout and pool waits: the preflight can wait/fail and the end-to-end request has no new deadline guarantee. This cost is explicit, not a measured speedup. It is proportionate only to the adopted product guarantee that a provably terminal-invalid receipt need not contend for a writer; independent plan review must accept it or return a concrete refinement. Timeouts, connection policy and budgets must not change to hide this cost. Place the read before existing current capture so its delay does not age the existing lease-time snapshot.

### Follow-up scope: paired snapshot connection ownership

The read-only scan found a concrete raw SQLite handle leak in `app/snapshot.py:create_snapshot`: in paired mode, the source connection is acquired before the destination, but the cleanup block starts only after both connections succeed. If destination acquisition raises, the paired snapshot error path cleans output files but leaves the source handle open. Scope is limited to `app/snapshot.py` and `tests/test_snapshot.py`; use `contextlib.closing` for both paired connections while retaining the existing backup transaction behavior, output validation, atomic publication, and original exceptions. Add a real-handle regression covering both main/relay roles and destination-open/destination-close failures, asserting original exception propagation, source-handle closure, and absence of outputs. RED before production edit, then focused and affected snapshot tests. This repairs connection ownership and does not attribute any prior timing failure.
